confidence_note: Verified in the full text. The book dates Kroc's visit to 1952; historical sources say 1954, so the year is omitted. The old text's 'Does McDonald's sell good hamburgers?' dialogue and 'McDonald's sells a system, not hamburgers' quote are not in the book; the real line is 'the hamburger wasn't his product. McDonald's was.' Book's revenue and store figures are left out because they are dated.
facts: A fifty-two-year-old milkshake machine salesman, Ray Kroc, walked into a hamburger stand in San Bernardino, California, run by two brothers, to sell them a milkshake machine.
Gerber writes that the stand worked 'like a Swiss watch': hamburgers made quickly, efficiently, inexpensively and identically, and anyone could do it.
Kroc watched high school kids working with precision under the owners' supervision while long lines of customers waited.
He convinced the brothers to let him franchise their method and later bought them out.
Gerber: franchising was over a hundred years old; Kroc's innovation was the Business Format Franchise, which hands the franchisee a whole system of doing business, not just a name.
'What Ray Kroc understood at McDonald's was that the hamburger wasn't his product. McDonald's was.' The franchisee wanted to know one thing: 'Does it work?'

Because franchisees left to their own devices would fail, Kroc built a systems-dependent business, not a people-dependent one, a business that could work without him; he 'went to work on his business, not in it,' like an engineer on a pre-production prototype.

When the pie-shop owner Sarah objected that her aunt would see McDonald's as the opposite of a model, Gerber answered that McDonald's keeps its promise every time, and that her aunt had one kitchen while Kroc had thousands.
scene_details: a salesman carrying a milkshake machine into a hamburger stand
high school kids flipping burgers with precision while long lines wait
the aunt's single kitchen against thousands of kitchens
tension: A salesman came to sell one machine and left wanting to sell the whole stand's way of working.
opening_idea: Start with a 52-year-old milkshake machine salesman stepping into a San Bernardino hamburger stand and watching teenagers work.

lessons.idea: Treat the way your work gets done as something you can write down and hand over, so the result stays the same when you are not there.
lessons.anchor: Teenagers produced identical burgers because the method, not one cook, carried the quality.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A café owner writes a one-page opening routine so any new barista can open the shop the same way.

reflect_final: Which task that only you know how to do could someone else do tomorrow if you wrote down its steps tonight?

use_cases.situation: A recurring task always waits for one colleague.
use_cases.move: Suggest writing the steps down so a newcomer can do it, the way Kroc's teenagers made the same burger.

use_cases.situation: You're about to go on holiday and fear the inbox.
use_cases.move: Write a one-page 'how this runs without me' note and test it on a colleague before you leave.

use_cases.situation: A relative runs a small shop and is never off.
use_cases.move: Ask which one routine could be written down so someone else can do it the same way.

pocket_idea: Kroc didn't sell the burger; he sold a kitchen that works the same in anyone's hands.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Ray Kroc walked into a burger stand to sell a milkshake machine and realised the stand's routine was the real product.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: A 52-year-old milkshake machine salesman visits a burger stand in San Bernardino. High school kids are making identical burgers fast, cheap, like a Swiss watch. He talks the brothers into letting him franchise the method. Gerber's point: the hamburger wasn't Kroc's product. The business that worked without him was.
